utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I was not informed about any preliminaries. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The Chamber received notice of extended cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony on Thursday. Mr. Zec will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Zec, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you were working as a lorry driver in a company in Prijedor in 1991 when you were mobilised and sent to Croatia as a part of the 5th Battalion of the 343rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade. The commander of the 5th Battalion was Slobodan Kuruzovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have up on the screen, 65 ter 32003.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vujic, this is an article from Kozarski Vjesnik from May 1994 about appointment of Slobodan Kuruzovic to manager of Kozarski Vjesnik. In the text below the photo, you will see it says on 16 September he joined the 343rd Motorised Brigade, also says that he was in command of the 5th Battalion, commander of Serbian TO, member of the SDS. So this is Slobodan Kuruzovic, your commander in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a Slobodan Kuruzovic who was then a member of the brigade. He still hadn't become the commander of any Territorial Defence. He was a member of the war-time 343rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: While you were in Croatia, member -- commander of the 343rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade was Vladimir Arsic; right.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: After you returned to Prijedor, you say upon orders of Commander Arsic, you formed a unit composed of mainly Serb-dominated areas of Prijedor. This unit, Mr. Vujic, later became battalion of the 43rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct that I was given the task to establish a unit where there were Serbs only. Puharska was also in my area of replenishment and the population was 98 Muslim, and there were a few villages that were also almost purely Serb populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's in your statement. I was more referring to that battalion which later became part of the 43rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade of the VRS. That's right; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't later practically. Rather, from the first soldier who was given the task to establish it joined the 343rd Motorised Brigade, practically automatically whoever responded to mobilisation became a member of the 343rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you already told us you were commander of this battalion. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I was commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Arsic, he was commander of the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your command post, you say, was in Serena [phoen] tile factory, that's across the road from Prijedor hospital and about half a kilometre away from Keraterm; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you said now is incorrect. My command was in an abandoned building of a ceramic tile factory called Serena, so that has nothing to do with rubber or tires. It is correct that it was perhaps a bit less than a kilometre away from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In your dealings with military issues prior to the conflict and establishing your unit, you were engaged in activities to provide weapons to Serbs in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, among other things. That is to say, all of those who wanted to join the war-time unit were supposed to be equipped and armed. My logistics base was the garrison. That is to say, all of those who came and became members of this unit had to be armed and were armed. I personally handled some of that, as well as my assistants, because from day one, I set relations of hierarchy within that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You were in contact and you worked on these issues together with SDS and JNA officials, such as Kuruzovic, Arsic, and Zeljaja; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superior command was the command of the 343rd Motorised Brigade, as it was known at the time, and I co-operated with the population that were SDS members to a large extent, so it was impossible to do anything there without the presence of members of the SDS and even their officials at different levels, that is to say, at local commune level and municipality level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were not asked who was in command. Could you please answer the whole of the question. Did you work together with SDS? I think you dealt with that. Did you work together with JNA officials in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. That was my superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did those include Kuruzovic, Arsic, and Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you also attended meetings with SDS officials to discuss this military organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already had an opportunity to answer this question. I said that I was not a member of the SDS and on that basis I never attended. However, as for military matters, I did attend certain meetings that were attended by the top people of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 10842. And this is a book of minutes of the SDS Prijedor Municipal Board. We need English page 100, B/C/S page 141. There is no date for this meeting but we know it is from this December 1991 because, in this book, the meeting held prior to this one was held on 2nd December and the one after was on 27 December 1991. The title is: "Meeting of the representatives of the Prijedor municipality sector for military matters." It starts by noting that 18 members were present. Simo Miskovic, president of the Prijedor SDS Municipal Board, opened the meeting with a presentation of the instruction from the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is a list of ten items, and below number 10 it says: "The above represents the first stage of preparations ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These tasks, Mr. Vujic, also appear in a document called A and B instructions issued by the Bosnian Serb leadership on 19 December 1991, and at this meeting these instructions were introduced in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to see this document so now I'm in a position to give an exact answer to this. You can see that this is a meeting of the representatives of the representatives of the authorities with regard to military matters and that is the basis upon which I was present there. I do not recall the political issues that were dealt with there, but I see that this had to do with instructions that were adopted by the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska and the chairman familiarized all present with that, so I was included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. -- you already answered the question. You were present at this meeting. That's clear; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I couldn't remember whether I attended this meeting, but as I saw this document I realised that I was present. It is possible that I even came during that part of the meeting when the military organisation was being discussed, so that's the reason why I don't remember the meeting from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would note that this excerpt of this meeting is in evidence as P3960. Can we have on the screen 65 ter 32523. And this is an article from bulletin of the 43rd Brigade. In English just below middle of the page, in B/C/S in the middle of the left column, it says: "Commander of this battalion, Drasko Vujic, a man who was among the first who felt the fascist vibrations of the centuries-old enemies said, People of Potkozarje know very well how it feels to suffer the war atrocities and fascist evil deeds. This is why we had to avoid the fate of our grandfathers. We had to be ready for when they come. The old mistakes had to be avoided."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, the reference to the war atrocities and the fate of our grandfathers is the reference to the Second World War and crimes against Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is only the Second World War that is being talked about and the crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And when you say "we had to be ready for when they come, the old mistakes had to be avoided," so you were referring to the process of arming and forming units that we were discussing a moment ago; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that happened at the time indicated that unfortunately this unfortunate war was in the making. And only those who didn't want to understand this and could not understand this had to prepare. All normal people had to prepare, knowing the horrors that civil war brings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 7 that your unit participated in mopping up of Kurevo and that -- and you say you did not go to Brisevo. Apart from your unit, Mr. Vujic, other units of the 43rd Brigade, the 5th Brigade from Prijedor, and 6th Brigade from Sanski Most were also involved in these activities; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This axis where I took part as well, the units that you mentioned did not take part there. This axis was given this task. It was the 2nd Battalion and a smaller unit of mine had been attached to them. It was a reinforced platoon. It wasn't even a full company. Since it was being attached to other officers and placed under their command, I, as commander, did not allow them to go there without me, afraid of some kind of abuse for any reason, and that is how I happened to be in Kurevo during those two days during the mop-up operation there. We moved from the village of Ljeskare through Hambarine to Kurevo and went to the village of Raljas. Further on -- we didn't go any further. That was in the direction of Brisevo, but Raljas to Brisevo there's another 2 kilometres approximately. Brisevo on the other date -- yes, go ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I appreciate your attention to give all the details, but my question was more general, about operations in the whole area, including, Kurevo, Brisevo, other units also were involved in these operations, 5th Brigade from Prijedor, 6th Brigade from Sanski Most, among others; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the 5th Brigade did not participate. Had you an allowed me to finish that one single sentence, what I meant to say was that Brisevo was under the 6th Sana Brigade, and that is a complete answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these operations took a place in July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the 6th Brigade took part. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the direction of Sanski Most and Ostra Luka to the village of Brisevo. That's where the 6th Brigade participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Apart from Brisevo, in late July 1992, other areas of Prijedor were mopped up, including Carakovo, Zecovi, Biscani and other locations; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes. But I don't know any details because I didn't participate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you were aware, were you not, that large numbers of non-Serb civilians were killed in these operations by members of your brigade, among others; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I didn't know at the time. I found out about many things later when I spoke to my colleagues and also at a briefing at the brigade commander's. That operation was mentioned, too, where quite a few civilians fell victim as well. Also, quite a few people from that area were taken to Keraterm and Omarska and some were taken to Trnopolje as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And when you say that there was a briefing at the brigade command, that's in 1992, shortly after these operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not as soon as you think, but I'm sure that it happened after two months. And that thing was also mentioned during our briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you are also aware, were you not, that the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina confirmed conviction against members of the VRS and police, including Dragoje Soldat, member of your brigade, for the killing of Muslims in Carakovo in front of the mosque after which they burned up the mosque; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Soldat et al case is something that I've been familiar with for half a year. Now, at the time when things were happening I didn't know anything. Knowing Soldat, I can say that he was one of the military policeman. I couldn't believe that he would have been capable of participating in any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one asked you whether you believed to be true what the court had decided. Just whether you were aware of it, and you've answered that question. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Similarly you are aware, are you not, that 15 other members of Serb forces currently awaiting trial for the killing of 29 Muslim civilians in Zecovi in late July 1992 which were killed as part of this operations; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that after the event of 30th May, which you referred to as the attack of Prijedor, Serb forces attacked the nearby area of Prijedor called Stari Grad, destroyed a mosque, demolished houses, rounded up civilians and took them to camps. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before you finalize your question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were pretty patient with this -- "this Chamber received evidence." How could this witness know which evidence this Chamber receives. If he wants to [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic, it is an announcement. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's just confusing because after the testimony of many my witnesses, they were so confused with this statement. They didn't know what they were supposed to answer, whether they should know that. And then they blamed me, why I didn't introduce what Chamber knows to them so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you explained to them that they were not expected to know what evidence had been led and you explained them what that question aimed at, isn't it? Mr. Zec, if there's any confusion -- and you interrupted already immediately when Mr. Zec had only started to put to the witness what he wanted to put to the witness. Let me see. Your question, "were you aware of this," Mr. Zec, is ambiguous. You should clearly ask whether the witness was aware that the Chamber received such evidence or whether the witness was aware of the events having happened on which the Chamber had received evidence. And it would always be good to -- if you refer to evidence to assist Mr. Lukic by just briefly referring to what evidence you are pointing at. So what would you like to hear from the witness? Whether he was aware that the Chamber received that evidence; or whether he was aware of these events having happened? Make it clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will and thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, this Court has heard evidence about the events in the area of Prijedor called Stari Grad - some of which can be found in P3414, paragraph 20; P480, pages 9 to 12 - that after the events of 30th May 1992, Serb forces attacked Stari Grad, destroyed the mosque, demolished houses, rounded up non-Serb civilians, took them to the camps. So were you aware of this happening in Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object again, Your Honours. How would these numbers should help the witness understand what he was asked? If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The numbers are to assist you, Mr. Lukic. I invited the Prosecution, I said it would be good that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not answering the question, Your Honour. Why should he assist me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you that have an opportunity to prepare for re-examination and that you are able to follow whether Mr. Zec accurately or not accurately points at evidence this Chamber received, Mr. Lukic. So that you have an opportunity to intervene on a proper basis. That's why it is said and that is why I invited Mr. Zec to do that so that you can verify whether Mr. Zec when putting to the witness what evidence this Chamber received, that you have an opportunity to -- to respond -- to tell us that Mr. Zec, if he would do so, is not properly presenting that evidence. Because that would be a proper reason for an objection. This is my ruling. Could the witness please answer the question: Were you aware of these events happening at the time, the events Mr. Zec described as having been brought to the attention of this Chamber through the evidence he identified? And you don't have to worry or bother about the numbers. That was for Mr. Lukic. Were you aware at the time that these events were happening or had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I answer by just yes or no, I can say yes, I knew. But a short explanation will not take up that much time. It is incorrect that after that the Serb forces attacked Stari Grad. The fighting started from the centre and continued across Stari Grad and that's where they ended. The Muslim paramilitary formations that had attacked the town were also engaged in fighting and they were withdrawing through Stari Grad, they opened fire from there, and that's why fighting continued there and ended there. That's the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And to be perfectly clear what you're saying -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the Rules are changing now. If we wanted to present with the Prosecution witness during our cross-examination, we had to show the evidence we want to use. We were not able just to give a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- sweeping statement about the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if there's any reference which you consider not to be accurate, then, of course, you can invite Mr. Zec. Mr. Zec, would you please be so kind as to put the evidence or this or that evidence to the witness and then we'll decide on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly what we asked, to follow the same rules we had to follow during our cross-examinations. If something is used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you like to be shown to the witness at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whatever they use with the witness. Whatever -- they cannot be sweeping statement. "This Chamber is -- heard the evidence," that is just confusing the witness every time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Defence never did that and that the Defence was always stopped when doing that? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We always showed the evidence. We would say "this is our position" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not my --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but not "the Chamber received the evidence." We never used that. And it was just imported from the Karadzic case when the part of Karadzic OTP members joined our trial. That's when this practice is introduced to this trial. Never before. Not by the OTP, not by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're referring to what the Defence did during its case. Of course, the Defence is -- as a starting point, free within, of course, the context of whether it's examination-in-chief, whether it's cross-examination, to put to the witness as they wish. I asked you when were you stopped doing that. The Chamber would be assisted, because you say we changed the rules. So therefore I would like to receive an answer to my question at what point in time you did put such references to the evidence to the witness and when you were stopped so that we can review that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We never stopped because we never started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's your own free choice to do that, isn't it. You can put the questions -- you put a question to a witness. Then that question is not objected to or objected to. If it's not objected to then you just proceed. If you have chosen never to put such a question to the witness, then it's difficult to say that we changed the rules because it never happened. And therefore if you say, We were never stopped because we never put such a question to the witness, within, of course -- I must be clear, of course, within the context of what can be put to a witness in examination-in-chief and cross-examination as far as leading is concerned. That's, of course, a matter which should still be considered. Mr. Zec at this moment is cross-examining the witness. Mr. Lukic, if you want to further follow up this, you can make submissions, either brief oral submissions or written submissions, on this subject in which you substantiate your objections. We'll now move on, Mr. Zec, to the extent possible. Where Mr. Lukic considers it fair to the witness to put some of that evidentiary material, you're invited to consider whether that would be wise to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I add something, Your Honour. I can add maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one more line --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then we will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were instructed to present to the witness the evidence we want to use or to confront the witness with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In examination-in-chief or in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In cross-examination. We were always instructed and I think I -- we can find that ruling [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I answer him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also depends on what exactly is put to the witness. But Judge Moloto would like to add a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed it is part of cross-examination in the adversarial system, that during cross-examination you've got to put your case to the witness. And what Mr. Zec is doing is precisely that. He's putting the position of the Prosecution to the witness for the witness to comment on that, if he knows anything about it. Now, how do you it, is your choice. If you do it by giving him a piece of paper or you do it by telling him that the Chamber has received a certain kind of evidence, that's a stylistic situation. It depends on the counsel who is doing the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also depends on the subject matter. If it is a detail in a document, then, of course, you put that document to the witness. If it is a more overall picture of events which occur during a couple of days, then you may choose another -- another technique. And there's always an opportunity for the other party to object to that, and then depending on the situation we find ourselves in, the Chamber will rule on that. We said one more line as I -- I invited you to make further submissions, if you wish to do so. We'll now continue to hear the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, sorry for this long delay. On page 13 of today's transcript, you explained what you knew about the Stari Grad operation on 30th May 1992. But my question was: Were you also aware that during the course of these operations, the mosque was destroyed, houses were destroyed, civilian -- non-Serb civilians were rounded up and taken to camps? Were aware of these events as well?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when that happened and immediately after that I didn't know. Later, when I toured the area, I saw the consequences of fighting in Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You talk in your statement about the mosque in Puharska. This mosque was destroyed in late August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 9 that the mosque was destroyed in a strong explosion which you could hear from your home a kilometre away. That's what you say and that's what you could hear; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Shortly after, there was another explosion in which the Catholic church in Prijedor town was destroyed, and you could hear that explosion as well; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it, but I didn't know where it was coming from and what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But you learned shortly after that the Catholic church was destroyed in the same night as the mosque; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning hours of that day, I learned that the Catholic church had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Zekerijah Kusuran, who you say was among those who organised the handover of weapons - this is transcript page 34961 - and his wife died in the explosion of the mosque; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Rasim Dzafic was injured in the explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was seriously injured by the pieces of glass that had shattered in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me show you photographs of the mosque which you have seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up, I would like to put one question to the witness. A minute ago, you said: "I saw the consequences of fighting in Stari Grad," and that was in response to Mr. Zec's information about the mosque destroyed, houses were destroyed, non-Serb civilians were rounded up and taken to camps. Would you qualify these events as normal consequences of fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that there was fighting. You could easily see that on the houses and on all the other features. That's why I said that I had seen consequences of fighting. I don't know what happened to the population. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You started your responses to Mr. Zec when he asked you: "Were you aware of these events as well." And then you said: "Yes, yes." And then later you referred to the consequences of fighting, of combat. So this is -- again, do you consider this -- these events to be normal consequences of combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To Mr. Zec's question, as if I knew -- or, rather, he said that the Serbian forces after the attack on Prijedor attacked Stari Grad, and my answer was that that was not after but during the fighting. And I said that I knew that there was fighting going on there. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This -- on the screen, we have file related to the destruction of the mosque in Donja Puharska and, for the record, 65 ter 31821. Can we have English page 12, B/C/S page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So we see here the house of Rasim Dzafic after the explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an occasion to see this photo during my previous testimony and my answer then was that I thought that indeed was Rasim Dzafic's house. Although I had to say that there were hundreds of such houses in Puharska. However, my answer was yes and still is yes, this is Rasim's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have English page 13, B/C/S page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is the house of Zekerijah Kusuran after the explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter says "Zekerijah Kusturan" but his name was - just a moment - Kusturan, Kusturan, yes. And this is his house, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have English page 6, B/C/S page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the mosque in Donja Puharska before it was blown up; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have English page 9, B/C/S page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is the mosque after it was blown up; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that this is that particular mosque. Not based on this picture. But I can say that parts of the mosque were destroyed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have English page 11, B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, here, we see remains of the mosque being cleared away by the Prijedor public utility company; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see a building machine clearing the rubble. I don't know when that happened. I've not seen this photo before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, earlier you said parts of the mosque were destroyed. Which parts were -- remained intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the witness can remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness -- he said, "I said," so it may be that he now resolves the matter, Mr. Lukic, there's a chance. Could you please repeat what you started to say. You said what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that photo shows parts of a mosque. You can see a minaret. But based on that photo, I couldn't tell you which mosques those part belonged to, which mosque that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So when you were using the words "part of the mosque," then you were referring rather to what can be seen on the photograph, then that it refers to what you say happened to that mosque and you don't even know whether the pictures are about that mosque in Donja Puharska. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I was saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have English e-court page 5, B/C/S -- English e-court page 7, B/C/S e-court page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you recognise on this photo remains of the mosque and in the background is the house of Zekerijah Kusuran? Can you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise the things that you have mentioned in this photo, but it is very obvious that the photo depicts a site of major destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please Mr. Zec -- please, Mr. Lukic, is there any dispute about whether the photographs, apart from how it all happened, but these photographs depict the mosque of -- after destruction. I'm just limiting it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We cannot confirm that, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it could be any mosque, not necessarily this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not familiar and we did not have any means to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have an expert on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I have a question. Can I ask the witness a question. Sir, Mr. Vujic, apart from this photograph, are you aware of the extent of the destruction of the mosque after the incidents that are being discussed here? And if so, can you tell us how -- what that extent is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best answer would be that the mosque was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's the right time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back after 20 minutes. We'll take a break first. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Zec, as far as timing is concerned, another -- little bit over half an hour? Is that what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I believe so. In my time -- certainly I won't go above my estimated time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you said you needed another one hour and a half, I think, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Certainly won't go over that. I hope I will be finished even shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Vujic. Mr. Zec will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, before you break we were talking about Donja Puharska in the summer of 1992. Last week when Mr. Lukic asked you about Puharska, you explained that people continued to live there and you said that Puharska was densely inhabited area with some 5.000 people living there. You said 98 per cent of Puharska population were Muslims. This is transcript page 34964 through -67. So, to be clear, these 5.000 Muslims in Puharska, you were referring to Donja Puharska in the period after the Serb take-over of Prijedor. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a mistake in translation or interpretation? But that's not correct. I said that Puharska had a population of almost 5.000. 35, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It may be translation. I said 5.000. I think we are on the same page. Thank you. You also talked about mopping up of Puharska after the Muslim attack on Prijedor. In paragraph 12 of your statement you say upon orders of the brigade, your units searched Puharska for suspects of the attack and for unknown Muslims from Hambarine and Kozarac who were seeking refugee with their relatives in Puharska suspected of having taken part in clashes. These searches for suspects, Mr. Vujic, resulted in rounding up of Muslims in Donja Puharska. Men were taken to camps while women, children and elderly were taken to Muslim-held territory in Central Bosnia. That was the reality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one day after the attack of Muslims on Prijedor, Puharska was searched. The reason why is precisely what you referred to just now. Part of their armed forces had withdrawn through Donja Puharska. They fled. Because that's the way they came when they carried out the attack. The estimate was that many of them stayed on there and that they found refuge there. Even before that, those who were fighting in Kozarac reached Puharska in some way and found refuge there. That was the main reason for the search of Donja Puharska. Some of our units took part in that. My unit had the task of securing part of the zone that links Puharska to another part of the local commune of Prijedor too, where the small river of Puharska is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the reality was that those who were seeking refuge in Puharska, they were rounded up, taken to camps. Women, children were taken to the Muslim-held territory. That's was happening there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did not happen then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31822.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you a local statement of Fikret Hodzic dated 15 July 1997. It's on the screen. At the beginning of the statement he talks how at the end of May 1992, he moved from Kozarac to Prijedor. Page 2 in English, he said he was in Donja Puharska in his aunt's house for about a month. In the middle of the page he explains how initially only Bosniaks who had found refuge in Donja Puharska were expelled, leaving the local population alone. He said: "They took the men from these settlements to the Trnopolje camp and the women, children and elderly were sent in the direction of Travnik. They took us to Trnopolje by bus." He said: "When I came to the Trnopolje camp, I found several thousands imprisoned Bosniaks and Croat there." So, Mr. Vujic, this was the reality: Muslims in Puharska, Donja Puharska were rounded up, detained, and expelled. That was happening; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement says things that are the direct opposite of your first question. The first time you said that they were expelled from Puharska somewhere to Central Bosnia. Now, in this statement, this is not mentioned at all. Because men -- please do allow me to explain so that I could be ready to answer your further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Travnik was in Central Bosnia area. People were taken there. Whether it's Travnik or somewhere else, that's not relevant. People were taken into this direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do allow me to respond in two sentences. That day when the search was carried out, part of the men were taken away. In a previous statement I corrected myself. My first knowledge was that they were about 30 of them, but later on I received some information and I received convincing information that there were about 60 of them. They were taken on two buss to the camp of Omarska. Civilians, women, children, they were not touched then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they touched at any later point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, civilians were never expelled in that way. Rather, an action took place and they had the opportunity to say whether they wanted to leave. Some of them wished to go to Trnopolje because from there they could go very easily and quickly to third countries, and some stated other views, how they wished to leave. There were many reasons. But there was not a single reason that they were intimidated, beaten, et cetera. However, it was hardship. They were without money, they were not -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I asked you is whether they were touched at any later point in time. What I do understand is that you say they were never touched. They were free to go. If they wanted to go to Trnopolje, fine. If they wanted to go elsewhere, that was fine as well. You followed their wishes. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. That is what I took part in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking only about what you took part that but what happened. Were there any members of the civilian population which were not free to choose where they wanted to go? Apart from -- irrespective of whether you were involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that they -- they left because they wished to do so. When did that happen? Because that the whole starting point of my question. When did that happen? And let's start with Trnopolje. When did they, who wished to go it Trnopolje as you told us, when did they go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trnopolje was established during combat operations in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you when it was established. I asked you when the population you were referring to went to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never did the entire population go at one point in time, so it's very hard to answer that question of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. When did the first ones -- when did the majority go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know because they left without me knowing about this. In the month of September, I was no longer in Prijedor. All of those who left after September -- well, of course, I had no contact with them. I was at the front line with my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before September, wasn't there a large number that went to Trnopolje before September? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly how many left, but some did leave. I knew that. But I was never present when they were leaving and they didn't ask for my assistance to get to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, earlier you said -- you took part in -- if they want to go to Trnopolje, fine, you said. If they wanted to go elsewhere - that's what my question was - that was fine as well. You followed their wishes, and then you said: "Yes, of course, that is what I took part in." Now could you tell us exactly then what you took part in? What did you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My task as a soldier did not have to do with anything that related to civilian affairs. When they were leaving, it was the civilian authorities with -- that were organising with the assistance of the police these buses in Donja Puharska, and those who wanted to leave left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us, first of all, that they didn't leave at the time but later you told us that you don't know, as a matter of fact, who left before September in what numbers. And then I asked you whether I understood you well that they were all free to go wherever they wanted to go, Trnopolje, elsewhere. And then you said: "Yes, of course, that is what I took part in." I asked you what you did. If you say, I take part in this, then I'm a bit puzzled if on my next question you say, I had nothing to do with it because it was all civilian affairs. So tell us what you meant when you said that you took part in this voluntary moving-out either to Trnopolje or elsewhere. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that I ever stated that I took part in that part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please -- please do allow me to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, you've said it. We'll verify it. If you say, That's not what I said, then we'll listen to the audio and we'll have it verified that -- whether you said or not and we'll fully accept if you didn't say so. Usually the Defence is also listening to the B/C/S channel so usually if there's something mis-recorded, they will inform us. But if you say, It's not what I said, then we'll verify it. Is that what you want us to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for checking this. I trust you. But also I have the right to say that I do not remember having said that. However, of course, if there is proof that I said this, I will explain what I meant. When I said that in some way I did take part, it did not pertain to this, that I was directly transporting these people to Trnopolje or elsewhere. My participation in Donja Puharska was constant communication with the population. That is how I knew who wished to leave, who kept silent and perhaps did want to go, who wanted to intimate to me that they would leave as soon as they were given the opportunity to do so. I remember this one organised departure in front of the local commune centre of Puharska. Those who wished to leave gathered there and the civilian authorities organised transportation and I know of that event. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transportation to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transportation to Trnopolje. To the collection centre of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe, maybe, the month of August, beginning of August. I know it was warm. It was hot. But I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, as a result of these activities and, as you say, wishes of the people to go, out of total of 5.000 people, Muslims who lived in Donja Puharska in mid-May, as you say, by 1993 this number was reduced down to 1.000; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's my question. Out of 5.000 Muslims in Puharska in mid-May -- in mid-1992, as you say, by 1993 there was only 1.000 Muslims in Donja Puharska; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. My knowledge says the direct opposite, that most of them remained in their homes until 1993. Although, as I said, after September 1992 I was not present there in Prijedor. However, I came to Prijedor from time to time and that was not the impression that I got, that so many of them had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 65 -- actually P number, it's P7126. And this is an overview of the 1993 census in Prijedor broken down to local communities prepared by the Serb authorities in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if you see item number 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- it's Donja Puharska --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which authorities in Prijedor, if we can hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, do you -- could you give us more information about the document, who --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's in evidence. We can pull out more information but my understanding it was even seized from Prijedor authorities in -- within government offices in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is in evidence. I don't know whether you objected at the time, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Your Honour, because there is no any trace what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently I don't remember, as a matter of fact, but apparently we admitted into evidence. That means that on the basis of that decision Mr. Zec can put questions. If there's anything to be revisited in terms of authenticity or source, then, of course, new facts we would hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, item number 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry. Only it was presented that it was done by authorities from Prijedor, so it has to be presented differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is in evidence, so Mr. Zec can put this document to the witness. Witness, this is a report about the numbers of people living in the various parts of Prijedor municipality, I do understand. Carefully listen to the question Mr. Zec will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in response to Mr. Lukic, Mr. Traldi just reminded me that was Mr. Lukic's witness, Vladimir Lukic, who confirmed that this census was conducted as a response to request from the government. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any recollection, Mr. Lukic? We'll check that. You'll understand that if you elicited that evidence yourself, then it's not the best way of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, you elicited the evidence but from a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct. I'd elicited on cross-examination from Vladimir Lukic the evidence that the government had conducted a census in 1993, that he was aware, he and his government were aware of the results and the demographic change and the extent of it in municipalities specifically including Prijedor. The Chamber has also received Kozarski Vjesnik publishing the results of this census, though not on a location by location basis, which I informed Mr. Lukic when this issue came up during Witness Puhalic's testimony and I understand that the matter had been resolved at that time. But in case there is any further question about it, I can provide him specific references at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, sufficient information about the background?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still I have a problem presenting this, "this is done by Prijedor authorities," because I cannot see it from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's leave it. Witness, this is a 1993 census. We leave out at this moment the details. And it is local, about Prijedor. Carefully listen to Mr. Zec's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, item number 5 is entry for Donja Puharska. Number for Muslims is 1.073. So this was the result of the reduction of Muslims in Donja Puharska. Out of 5.000 in mid-1992, down to 1.073 in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to start answering because you're not allowing me, but this was no census in 1993. This is analytical information that was compiled by someone on the basis of memory or a free estimate. You asked me about Donja Puharska and here's the proof. It says here that in Donja Puharska, the population was 3.107, and just now we said that there were 5.000. Now from 5.000 it should have fallen to 1.000, not 3.000. Obviously this information is not correct. And I'm sure and I claim that there was no census carried out in 1993. There was no one to go from house to house and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, let's be clear. You told to Mr. Lukic that there was 5.000 Muslims in Donja -- in Puharska and you said 98 per cent of them were Muslims. I asked you today to confirm that and you confirmed that 5.000 of Muslims lived in Donja Puharska. Now, I presented you with this census and it says 1.000 of Muslims in Puharska. And I'm telling you this is the result of the reduction of Muslims in Puharska that was conducted in the matter of several months. That was the reality at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that this document is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not relevant. And I'm putting it to you like you're putting things to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, relevance is for us to decide. What can you tell us about the document? You say it was not -- who drafted it? How was it done? Because you say it's not valid. What do you know about the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have told you that there was no census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you told us a minute ago that this document was based on the recollection of individual persons giving an assessment of numbers. Now, in view of the detail, that is, to say the least, not very plausible, but because you told us that that is what it is, I asked you what do you know about -- who drafted this document; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of what data was it compiled? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I don't know. But I know that it is not based on a census. And it says in the title that this is a census, the 1993 census. Sir, there was no census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- I leave it to the parties to discuss whether or not there was something which you could or could not call a census. But at this moment it's clear that you don't know who authored it and you don't know on the basis of what it was compiled. The only thing you're telling us is you know that there was no census so it must be wrong. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question, please. Sir, based on your own knowledge, what's your estimate of the population numbers in 1993 in Puharska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you insist on me giving an arbitrary assessment, I will be honest and I will tell you that, all in all, there were about 1.000 people who left Puharska in 1993. Not more, according to my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So by simple arithmetic, according to you, having told us that before that there were 5.000, is it your position therefore that by 1993 there were 4.000 Muslims in Puharska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about 4.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, this reduction of Muslims and Croats in Prijedor is the result of crimes committed against non-Serbs by members of your brigade, among others, crimes of killings, destruction of property, communities, non-Serb religious sites. That was the reality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of this can apply to Puharska since no such thing happened in Puharska. Houses were not torched. People were not ill-treated. There were no crimes of that kind. I'm not ruling out some individual cases and we tried to prevent those as much as possible. Puharska is the same today as it was before the war. I believe that there is no more than 5 per cent of the total of newly built houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: During the course of the conflict, members of your unit publicly expressed hatred against other ethnic groups. You were aware of this; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an easy question to answer. My combatants realised that there was an enemy on the other side, an opponent. It was only logical that they were not supposed to love them or be kind to them. It was only logical for them to think how to save themselves from the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's look at an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 65 ter 32522. This is Kozarski Vjesnik from October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, may I urge you to answer the question. The question was not what internal feelings your people had but how they expressed themselves publicly. That was what the question was about. Carefully listen to the next question and try to answer the questions as put to you by Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look towards the end of the page in B/C/S, there's an article entitled: "We will make them disappear." In the second paragraph it says: "Vujic's soldiers told us that they were impatient to come to this front and defend the town [sic]." Several lines below in the same paragraph: "One of the officers, Petar Gagic said ... 'my Prijedor, our town. There is no longer any reason to be afraid. The men from Kozarac and many others have arrived and this will be a Serbian land once again. There is no more fear. We are chasing the Balija out. We will make them disappear.'" So, Mr. Vujic, this is an example of your officer expressing attitude of your soldiers towards other ethnic groups, in this case, Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object at this time. First, who is the author of the text. Second, was this confirmed by somebody who -- this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A lot of question -- lots of questions for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not even hearsay. This is fourth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is all nice questions for re-examination to rely on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is the author, first, if we can know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I said questions for re-examination. What -- Mr. Zec introduced this document as a publication in a newspaper. And I can imagine that there were a lot of questions about that and you certainly can put them to the witness. So, therefore, could you please answer the question, Witness? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question. Could the relevant part be zoomed in? I'd like to be able to see it better. And it is true that this was a member of my unit. I am familiar with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Please go on. He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could we zoom in in such a way -- and I do understand that it must be the first column of this. So if we could highlight that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, can you see better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your officer, Petar Gagic, said: "My Prijedor, our town. There is no -- no longer any reason to be afraid. The men from Kozarac and many others have arrived and this will be a Serbian land once again. There is no more fear. We are chasing the Balijas out. We will make them disappear." So this your officer expressing attitude of your soldiers towards other ethnic group; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question fully. If you will allow me, we arrived to defend Prijedor. Before that, already 13 municipalities fell. We were certainly determined to defend our town to the last man. Such were times. I told you how it happened. We were fighting against the Muslim forces aided by NATO pact. There were beasts, and it was only normal that my soldiers said that we would crush them. And I repeat that at this very moment. I share that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need more data. Who wrote this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a publication in a newspaper and that I have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe we would call the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- hesitation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- newspaper guy who wrote this, how he composed the text. What is his words, what is words from the guy who quoted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your objection is denied. The -- this document of which is not much more known than that it was a publication in Kozarski Vjesnik of the 16th of October, 1995, because that's what it says, is a newspaper article. We'll consider the probative value of this newspaper article in the context of the totality of the evidence and some of the observations you made, that is, that the author is not known, are all part of our assessment of what probative value should be given to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, did I say -- if I said the 16th, then it's because I have difficulties in turning my head to read the original date. 18th of October, 1995. Still, mid-October. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for an opportunity to say another sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, would you first not interrupt me, to start with. Once I've spoken, once Mr. Registrar have given the number, then you can ask whether you can add something. Mr. Registrar, I missed your -- the number you gave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, you wanted to add something. If it's brief and if it is directly related to -- to the questions that were put to you, you don't have to bother about authenticity or whether we should it admit or not because that decision has already been taken. So, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to add two more sentences on this issue. The Prosecutor asked me whether my fighters expressed hatred towards an ethnic group. An ethnic group implies both women and children as well as children and men and elderly, the whole ethnic population. We were attacked by women and children. We were attacked by men at arms. And this statement is relative to them, not to an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, you were not asked to give this comment. Second, if you say it's Serbian land, that reflects what -- that all non-Serbs apparently are not welcome at least, it's Serbian land. And that is not limited to men. That is not limited to soldiers. That is related to non-Serbs. That's at least my understanding. I give it to you so that you have an opportunity to comment on my understanding, that Serbian land is apparently for Serbs and not for non-Serbs, irrespective of gender and age.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A similar observation could be made as "Balijas to disappear." But I leave it to that. Mr. Zec will put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Vujic, consistent to this attitude of your soldiers, remaining non-Serbs of Prijedor were rounded up and many expelled, including, Dr. Ibro Beglerbegovic, who you mention in your statement, as well as your soldier Jasmin Zahidic and his family members; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an occasion to speak about Dr. Beglerbegovic and the events surrounding him. I don't know what happened to him at the time. In my statement I explained the relationship that existed while I was still in a position to communicate with him. As far as my soldier Jasmin Zahidic, I didn't know that at the time he was taken away in that way. What I knew then was that they wanted to leave Prijedor as soon as possible because they were members of the Roma, their life was not easy, and the majority of them wanted to go to a western country where they could enjoy benefits and live better. You asked me about Zahidic and that's why I'm telling all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And last week when I asked about Zahidic, you said he was your soldier and you were sure no -- none of your soldiers were ever expelled. Now you are telling to us that he was expelled. That's what you're saying to us; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a document before me so I can't tell you how long Jasmin remained my soldier. When -- once he was demobilised, he was no longer my soldier, so I don't know what happened to those who were no longer members of my unit. Zahidic provided his statement in Zenica and he never mentioned that he was a soldier. He said that he was a member of a work platoon which is a lie. In this list there is no single Muslim name of anybody who was a member of the work platoon. They were not registered as members of a war-time unit. They were registered in a different place as parts of a different record. He was not a member of the work platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, regardless of your soldier or Dr. Ibro, thousands of non-Serbs were rounded up and expelled from Prijedor area. That was the fact; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did leave Prijedor but I don't know under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Very quickly, P6925. And this is an article from Vreme dated 16 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Vreme, that's a Belgrade-based weekly magazine. You know that; right? Can you confirm that Vreme magazine, that was Belgrade-based? You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look in the article in front of you, it talks about Arkan's presence in the area of Krajina in 1995. English page 2, B/C/S first row, towards the bottom it refers to the operation launched in late September in which the area around Prijedor was cleansed of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please indicate where that can be found in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it's first row, towards the end of the first row. Still down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Shall we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Scroll down. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if you look towards the bottom of that box, Mr. Vujic, you will see it says: "According to the UNHCR reports, members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards expelled about 5.000 people to the territory under the control of the BiH government within only a few days. "According to the UNHCR, people were forced to swim across the river and many drowned during the attempt. Others died of exhaustion and beatings." So this is an example, Mr. Vujic, of public awareness of expulsions of non-Serbs from Prijedor area. So that was the reality at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I'm not aware of this publication. I also claim that at least 90 per cent of the population of Prijedor are not aware of it. Perhaps people in Belgrade were aware of it, if it is published in Belgrade. I don't know where the author of the article got his information from. I really never had an opportunity to hear or see what people in Belgrade wrote and read about Arkan and his army. In other words, I'm not familiar with this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is marked as MFI exhibit so I would ask that it be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object that it could be tendered through this witness after his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want to give you an opportunity to respond to the objection, but if you say you leave it to that, that's okay as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the interest of time I wanted to move on, but this topic is brought by witness and Mr. Lukic in his examination, so the exhibit relates to the topic and the witness confirmed that people were expelled from the area. In that sense, this exhibit is admissible through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As related to the events on which the witness himself testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He testified about Arkan and his army and his non-resubordination to his units. That's all he testified about Arkan. I don't remember that he testified about Arkan expelling civilians from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Awaiting a decision on the admission, the document should be marked for identification. The number would be, Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We have [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, we have a number already, yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's P6925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Focusing to Arkan for a moment, Mr. Vujic, Arkan's hostility against other ethnic groups was known many years before these events in Prijedor in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was afraid of Arkan, civilians, soldiers, Serbs, Muslims, everybody feared Arkan and his unit and his actions at all levels and in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Already in Croatia in 1991 when you were there, Arkan was making public statements in order to intimidate members of other ethnic groups. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Croatia, I didn't even know of Arkan's existence. I didn't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let me show you a clip depicting what Arkan said to an international correspondent in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 22456b.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if that can be played. We have provided transcripts. It's very short, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what are you -- are you establishing that he made such statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now this witness doesn't know anything about that. He says that he didn't know even that Arkan exists. So what's the use of -- because I take it that then you would want to put further questions to the witness or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On relation to Arkan and his attitude towards ethnic -- other ethnic groups during the war, I want to establish that this Arkan existed in 1991 and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness doesn't say he didn't exist. The witness says, "I was not aware of his existence." That's not the same as denying the exist of Arkan. He says, "I was not aware at that point in time of his existence," so there no need to put anything to him that Arkan did exist because the knowledge of the witness is not central here but it is the evidence before this Chamber, which leaves not much room to deny that Arkan existed at that point in time. Is that clear to you? I want ... you don't have to show it to the witness to let him admit that Arkan existed. There's no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It also has to do with Arkan's attitude toward ethnic -- other ethnic groups that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, but perhaps that's not the best to do that through this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay, I understand, Your Honours. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it doesn't relate to anything the witness told us directly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's clear. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Last week you told to Mr. Lukic with respect to the arrival of Arkan's Men to Krajina in 1995, that you did not know who they got tasks from and that it was clear to you that they did not -- that they were not receiving tasks from the army. This is at transcript page 34971. Mr. Vujic, this Chamber has received evidence about meetings General Mladic had with the highest police and military officials from the RS and Serbia discussing deployment of Arkan's Men. On 22nd September 1995, it was discussed that Arkan's Men were to arrest all those who were fleeing from the front; this is in P364, page 53. On 11 October 1995, Arkan's Men were instructed to make arrests in Prijedor; this is in P3094. So I take, Mr. Vujic, that you were not aware of these arrangements with respect to Arkan's activities in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
