utterances.text: I was not aware of any agreements between the army and Arkan. And I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. You are not aware of it. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm about to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very quickly then. Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Once you returned to Prijedor by 13 October 1995, your battalion joined Arkan's Men in combat operations in the area; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're not telling the truth. It's a major lie. I never joined Arkan's Men. I never even knew that his soldiers were engaged on that axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec put something to you. If you disagree, just say, I disagree. It's not the truth. Don't uses the word "lie." Mr. Zec presents what, in his view, is in evidence. If you disagree you can tell us. You are invited even to do so, but don't use words like: "That's a lie." It's put to you in order to seek either confirmation or denial. So apparently you disagree. You say your battalion did not join Arkan's Men in combat operations. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Very quickly I'm going to show you two documents in respect to your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is an order by the RS Ministry of Interior to Arkan's Men to stop arresting deserters and prepare for carrying out the combat tasks. This is 12 October 1995. Now we're going to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give the witness at least time to have a look at it briefly. Please read it, Witness. No need to say anything about it at this moment. Wait for the question after you have seen the next document. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 32521. And this is an article from Kozarski Vjesnik from November 1995. In the B/C/S, we need the article to the right side of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the upper part or in the lower part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Sorry, in the first column in the article -- this is -- this is -- this is the right article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In the first column of the article it says: "Enemy offensive was stopped. Members of the 43rd, 5th Kozarac and 6th Sana Brigades played a major role in this. Members of the police, part of which were Tigers from the Serbian Volunteer Guards, fought alongside them." So now if you look towards the end of the first column in your language, Mr. Vujic. In English it's at the end of the second column. It says: "We are here with a clear goal and task. For the time being" - and then next page in English - "we have completely carried out tasks." And at the end of this passage, there's a reference to you, Mr. Vujic, as a speaker. So you fought alongside Arkan's Men with a clear goal and task as presented in this article, and that was the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that there were two questions here. The first one has to do with the first document that you showed from me and from that I saw that this is a document that was issued by the minister of police on whose orders I cannot act and the army in general cannot act. I saw that it was sent to the Main Staff just by way of information, so that means that I disagree that General Mladic took part in that. Rather, he received this as information. As for this other part, I see that the author of this text is Vukasin Vukadinovic. He is a sports journalist, a commentator, and he has only been involved in sports. So it seems that the time has come for him to write about other things too, and this is his view of how the situation evolved and who took part in things. He certainly wasn't even close to the front line. But I'm going to tell you that I was on the main axis in defending us from enemy attacks. As I told you, I encountered a small unit of Arkan's there. We did not have any kind of co-ordinated action and we were not under a single command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I apologise. I tender these two documents and I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I would object to introducing this newspaper article. Regarding the document 32543, since it's signed by, allegedly -- I cannot recognise but signed by Tomislav Kovac, we do not have any objections to have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start then with the first one. Mr. Registrar that document would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 32543 will be Exhibit P7367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That one is admitted. Now the newspaper article, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe to wait until I have several questions about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's marked for identification and then we'll later decide on admission. Mr. Lukic, that will have to be done after the break because we'll take a break first. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher. We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I say that the newspaper article should be marked for identification, at least we would need a number. We are ignoring your important role, Mr. Registrar. Could you assign the number under which it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 32521 will be MFI P7368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, once again, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Zec, on page 47, line 3, put the following to you. I'm going to read it out in English so that you would get the right interpretation. Just listen carefully to what I'm saying. You cannot read it in English. I quote: [In English] "Mr. Vujic, this Chamber has received evidence about meetings General Mladic had with the highest police and military officials from the RS and Serbia discussing deployment of Arkan's Men. On 22nd September 1995, it was discussed that Arkan's Men were to arrest all those who were fleeing from the front; this is in P364, page 53." [Interpretation] I'd like us to take a look at what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to call up P364.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a diary and it is being asserted that it is General Mladic's diary. First I would like to show you page 51 because it's from the same meeting that was held on the 22nd of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 51 in both languages. [In English] There is a typed version of this document in B/C/S as well. If it's possible to have it, please, it's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have B/C/S on both sides of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just -- thank you, Your Honour. We'll wait. We have both versions now, and we need the last paragraph in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we see that this is a meeting of 22nd of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on page 49, Your Honour. If you want we can go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now can we go back to page 51 in English as well when we saw that it's from the 22nd September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last paragraph down here, General Gvero says: "Activities of paramilitary formations which are taking away household appliances. The following was seized from the 2nd Krajina Corps: 5 Pragas, 3 tanks, approximately 2 infantry companies, from Arkan's formation. The municipality of Sanski Most is controlled by many" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then the next page, please. [In English] Can we have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... wearing Arkan's uniform." Mr. Vujic, in relation to this, I would like to ask you the following. You, your men, at that point in time, did you have problems with members of Arkan's unit? Did they take your men? Did they arrest your men? Did they cut the hair of your men?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. I never encountered Arkan myself, but when I was at different fronts at the time when Arkan had certain activities in the area of Prijedor, when he arrested all military-age, able-bodied men. And often those who were not able bodied, he took them to the sports hall of Prijedor. He shaved their heads there. They experienced certain unpleasant things while that happened and then he took them to the front. Within some unit, I don't know which one, probably his, but I think that two of my soldiers were then on regular leave and they experienced that, so then I intervened and these two soldiers were returned to my unit. Had it not been for my soldiers, my intervention, I don't know what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. [Interpretation] Let us now go to page 53 that my colleague Mr. Zec mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have this page in my version so ... no, no, that's fine. In the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it says on this page: "300 of Arkan's volunteers arrive and were put into the RS MUP. They were reportedly meant to be behind the lines arresting all of those who are fleeing from the front." Now let us take a look at page 91 from this document. At this meeting from the 15th of October, 1995, that is the time-frame that is being referred to when the fighting is taking place around Prijedor, when the western Bosnian municipalities are falling, this is what Colonel Jakovljevic says, as written here: "People are openly asking who that was brought Arkan, and under whose patronage they are doing this. People are being beaten up, and yesterday they formed a gauntlet and beat everybody who came off the train." So we see that this is a meeting with the security organs. That is what is written here. And we see that the security organ that is referred to here as Colonel Jakovljevic does not know who it was that brought Arkan. Were you informed who it was that brought Arkan and under whose patronage he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any information as to who it was that brought Arkan, but I knew that he was within our police, that he had direct communication with Mr. Simo Drljaca, the chief of the police station, and I know that together Arkan's forces and our police forces intervened at Novi Grad when the time was critical. That is what I know about this situation. As for this other part, that soldiers were wondering who it was that brought Arkan, that's true. Everybody was wondering whether we needed him at all. I'm saying at that time and today and before that, Arkan and his men were not needed by me and my battalion for carrying out any mission whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same part, my colleague Mr. Zec says that the Trial Chamber has received evidence that General Mladic at meetings with the top police and military officials discussed the deployment of Arkan's Men. In addition to this document, Mr. Zec offered another document to you to support that, and that is document P3094. That is page 47, line 9. Let us now take a look at document P3094 that was shown to you by way of a general allegation that confirms Mr. Zec's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Since my name is mentioned I should have said that in my question I referred to this document as instruction to Arkan to make arrests in Prijedor. That's what I was referring to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, then it's even better, that creates confusion when that's -- this statement: "Mr. Vujic, this Chamber has received evidence," and this is in the same paragraph with the claim from the previous -- actually, the previous claim made by the Prosecution, that General Mladic had meetings with highest police and military officials from the RS and Serbia discussing deployment of Arkan's Men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're challenging that the Chamber received such evidence which would indicate this, and that would be a valid objection. That's not the objection you made at the time. You said that he should spell it out. But what you're telling us now is the evidence referred to by Mr. Zec does not present evidence of what he told us it would demonstrate. Now, that may have been a valid -- but that's not the objection you made. If there's a misrepresentation of the evidence, Mr. Lukic, in general terms or in specific terms you may object to that. Again, that's not what you did at the time. At the same time, I add to this, that there's no need to ask the witness questions about whether the evidence which was presented to the Chamber is supporting what Mr. Zec claims it to be. You can ask him about facts he is aware of, but not to challenge the misrepresentation of the evidence by Mr. Zec unless the witness has any specific knowledge about facts. If you would please keep that in mind, if you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, led me add just one sentence. What Mr. Zec said at that point in time, page 47, is, I quote: "On 11 October 1995, Arkan's Men were instructed to make arrests in Prijedor; this is in P3094." He didn't say who instructed -- who gave this order. He didn't say anything further and this is not deviating from the text we have in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, if you understand that in this same paragraph, this document should not be connected with the first sentence, that this Chamber has received evidence about meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I repeat what Judge Orie said, that was not your claim when you objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Physically I was not able to object. I did not know which the document is since we didn't see it. I had only the opportunity during the break to print the document, see the document. It was not possible for us to object to those statements "this Chamber has received evidence" and just telling us the numbers because there is a continuation of the examination which I have to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, was this document on the list you provided, that you would use in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and the meetings that Mr. Lukic is constantly referring to, that can be found in P364 in various pages and that was notified to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if the document was on the list of -- and that list was given to Mr. Lukic when? Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On Friday afternoon in the e-mail that we sent to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was sent after this gentleman finished his testimony on Thursday and I learn about it only this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This witness -- this witness continued his cross-examination today and -- Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If I just may add that our notification on Friday was as a result of direct -- the direct -- examination-in-chief from Mr. Lukic when he brought the issue of Arkan which was not provided and notified in the statement or 65 ter or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I think the parties have sufficiently exchanged their -- their views on this matter. Mr. Lukic, you may now continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just for clarification, Mr. Zec, is -- are we to understand that the meetings that you referred to are referred to in P364 and not in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This document [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because I thought Mr. Lukic is asking -- saying that this is a document that refers to meetings [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, with a lot of additional information, please continue your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujic, I apologise for having possibly contributed to the confusion. Now we've discussed something that may actually not concern you at all. I'm going to be mentioning some numbers you that also don't concern you but this will be done just for the record. On page 34978 of our transcript, you said that those people who were captured in Kozarac were taken to Keraterm by members of the VRS. How long did that process take?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, two or three days. For as long as combat activities were ongoing in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Keraterm was in the area from which your fighters hailed. You have told us that. Members of your unit were from that area. Did they guard Keraterm? Did -- when it comes to providing security for Keraterm, who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Keraterm was under the police exclusively. The military, i.e., the troops, did not have access to Keraterm at all. It was, indeed, in the area from which my members hailed. In the vicinity of Keraterm, the troops carried out their regular activities, but guarding Keraterm was not one of them. Nothing that the army did was relative to Keraterm. That's why my activities were very intense and I made sure that the troops did not approach that facility, that the troops didn't get involved because that would have meant that authorities would be confused and that would not have been in our favour at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did members of your unit interrogate those prisoners who were held at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 34979 of our transcript - and that was recorded on Thursday - lines 6 through 24, you spoke about a man who had brought a truck-load of people to Trnopolje. You said that he went back to bring some more people after that. Were you in a position to determine the ethnicity of the man who drove that truck and who had gone back to bring in some more people?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that opportunity. I could tell who that person was although we spoke only shortly. He was a Muslim. He had his own private truck. His private property. He was either from Kamicani or from Kevljani, I'm not sure. But I know that he had indeed driven a truck-load of women, children, and elderly people. He put some straw into the truck and that's how he drove them. When they left the truck, something impressed me. He said good-bye to a 10-year-old boy that was the exact same age of my son who was at home. I asked him if that was his son, and he said yes. And he also said that, I'm going back to get another truck-load of people because a lot of civilians were fleeing the area because of the conflict. That's how I want to help them, he said. That was some 10 kilometres away. That's all the conversation that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I had not seen the man before. He never introduced himself to me or the other way around. We just started talking without any formal introductions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the reason why you don't know from which village he hailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I couldn't tell that. But I know which village he brought those people from which is why I assumed that he hailed from the same village and that he was helping his neighbours and relatives by driving them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2 of today's transcript, line 16, you were asked who your commanders were. Perhaps I'm not right, but let me ask you whether Mr. Kuruzovic was one of your commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic was my commander in Western Slavonia; the commander of the 5th Battalion. I was a member of that battalion in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Prijedor -- or, rather, when he returned to Prijedor, do you know what formation Kuruzovic was a member of?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived a month and a half before Kuruzovic, and I received the task from the brigade commander to organise the population and place them under our control. When Kuruzovic arrived, he dismantled, disbanded his battalion. A lot of its members became members of our -- my unit and Kuruzovic remained as an operative in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about his link with the TO?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities issued a decision to set up the Territorial Defence. Since Kuruzovic was a prominent member of the SDS, they were of the opinion that he had enough experience, that he was a career officer, and that he could be put in charge as the commander of the Territorial Defence. That was an important role. He was thus appointed as the commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about that Territorial Defence? Was there just one Territorial Defence in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, there was a Territorial Defence but it was disbanded in all of its segments. It was assimilated into war-time units. The new Territorial Defence was then set up, but its objective was to place both human power and weapons under some sort of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That new Territorial Defence headed by Mr. Kuruzovic, under whose authority was it?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He received his tasks from the Executive Board primarily and the president of the municipality, i.e., from the executive powers. He also had good co-operation with the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown a document, P3960. We saw that you had meetings with SDS representatives and that you discussed military issues at those meetings. That was in December 1991, according to that document. Did you also have meetings with the Muslim side? If you did, when? Did you discuss the same issues?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often insisted on holding meetings with the representatives of Muslims from Puharska. Those were their official representatives, members of the former Territorial Defence who never became involved in the war-time units, nor did they ever hand in their weapons. I spoke about those activities on several occasions. There were a lot of efficient talks but some were very hard and any progress was hard to achieve. I tried very hard. Although I was dominant in every respect, I tried to show them that what we were offering them would have been beneficial, mutually beneficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also shown a document that I would like to call up as well, P7364.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek some clarification from your previous answer. I do understand from that meeting which was held in December 1991, that meeting in which it's recorded that instructions were referred to, that that information was not shared with the Muslims. Or was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the information was not shared with the Muslims. That was about organising the Serbian people. The Muslims had obstructed that in every sense. There were none of them present. That was the meeting that was held. And my comment consisted of just one sentence, and I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the reason why I'm asking this is that in the question and in your answer there's some kind of a suggestion that you meet equally with the Serbs as you met with the Muslims; whereas I do understand from your answer that when you met with the Serbs, it was purely an internal Serb affair. Whereas if you met with the Muslims, then by your mere presence it was already a kind of a conversation between two ethnic or two national groups, which is -- makes it different from your meeting with the Serbs of which the information was not shared ever with the Muslims. I'm putting this to you so as to give you an opportunity that where question and answer suggested that it was more or less the same, that you could look at it also from a different angle, and I would like to give you an opportunity to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you properly, obviously this is not about the same meeting. You can see from the minutes who was present and what the topic of the meeting was. However, the other meetings with the Muslims which were held on my initiative were conducted in order to prevent an armed conflict. They had weapons. I went as far as to pleading with their leader to make sure that our patrols got to know each other, to avoid shooting at each other, because once the first bullet is fired, there's no tolerance. There's no talks after that. That's the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call P7365.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, this will be a document about the destroyed mosque in Puharska. Would you please tell us, to the best of your knowledge, how many houses were either destroyed or damaged in Puharska when this explosion struck; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that three houses were destroyed and a dozen more in the close vicinity of the mosque were damaged. I'm referring to shattered window-panes and roof tiles. Those two or three houses that I mentioned first suffered more damage. The walls crumbled. The joinery was damaged. It was obviously a strong explosion, and it was initiated by laypeople who are not experts, then the results are what they are and what they were in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the three destroyed and some dozen damaged houses, how many more houses were either destroyed or damaged in Puharska during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand your question. I've already answered your question once. A very small number of houses were destroyed or damaged. Puharska still looks identical to how it looked before the war, during the war, and today. I've already stated in one of my statements that, as far as I know, less than 5 per cent of the houses are new. The rest are all old. This is yet another proof that property was not destroyed, that there was no destruction in Puharska whatsoever, and the main reason for that is that no active combat took place there, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who caused the explosion; could you tell us? Who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many people in Prijedor including myself don't know that. If you're interested if my opinion, I personally don't understand how come that so many services from all over the world have not been able to establish that. I only know that the person who did it was not an explosives expert. If I look at myself from the military point of view, if that had been done by an expert, there would have been a minor explosion causing the same effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that was intended, but you don't know whether it was a layperson or an expert who wanted to achieve that larger effect. You apparently do not know. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who did it and what the intention was. I'm telling you that according to the way I see, it was not done by an expert but by a layperson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's opinion and conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 26, line 18 of today's transcript, something was not recorded. You started explaining why people were leaving. It was recorded that people had no money and then you were interrupted. Could you tell us why people left Prijedor? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost overnight the situation became dramatic in Prijedor. Life became very hard. There was no electricity, there was no water. Companies closed down. Nobody received any salaries. The little that they brought from front lines was enough just for the bare necessities to provide for the families whereas the soldiers were fed by the army. The situation was very difficult. And if there had been a pool among the Serbs, I'm sure that 90 per cent of them would have also left. They would have gone looking for a new destination for themselves and their families. However, that was our reality and we took the crisis in our stride, and we made do as we best could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The only thing recorded here is what they brought from the front line, but it wasn't recorded what it was that they brought that was enough to provide for the livelihood of their families.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first soldiers received salaries, and during devaluation it could only be used on the first day or second day. The third day already you could only buy a pack of cigarettes or a loaf of bread for that entire salary. So soldiers were in a hurry. They didn't really receive the salary at the front. Specifically the personnel department of my battalion, they took this to the homes of the soldiers so that they could buy basic necessities so that people could survive for at least a week. But as I've already said, the soldiers themselves were receiving military rations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look at P7366 now, please. So we need the bottom of the page, the left-hand side in B/C/S. [In English] Bottom. Bottom left side, please. No, I need that. [Interpretation] I can't find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told who it was that said this, Petar Gagic. Was there a man like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the second paragraph of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So was there a Petar Gagic in your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he gave an interview to this journalist?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he gave an interview to this journalist. Not to him. Could you have this moved a bit so that I could see the author of this text?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no name.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, there is no name. He gave that at the moment when we arrived in Prijedor and the Ostra Luka front. The statement was made at that moment and you can see here that I'm speaking as commander, that the enemy had quite a large appetite, that we stopped then on time, that there is no need to be afraid and so on. I remember that Petar Gagic spoke in a very emotional way then. He said, Prijedor, home town of mine, don't be afraid. The men of Kozara are here. We are here. We are expelling the Balijas and we are not going to allow them to do this to us and we are going to destroy their seed. So we are defending ourselves from those who are attacking us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we move the B/C/S version to the left a bit so that we can see the right column. Further, please. Further. Stop. You see initials below the article. Are you familiar with these initials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is Zoran Sovilj because in the previous text it said Z. Sovilj. But it's possible that it's him. I don't know anybody else who could have written this kind of text, with these initials at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How has the family name of that person be spelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] S-o-v-i-l-j.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This text dated the 18th of October, you said that this was an interview that was given at the moment when you arrived Prijedor. At that moment where were the Serbs from Grahovo? So when you arrived in Prijedor, when you fought the Muslim units that were trying to enter Prijedor, at that moment where were the Serbs from Grahovo? Are they still in Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I found out from the commander, and that was the task I was given, that Prijedor is not being defended by a single unit, that there was general disarray, that 30 municipalities fell in a very short period of time, and that the army and people were withdrawing. Those who remained could not or did not want to fight, unfortunately, ended their lives in the most tragic possible way. Prijedor was not defended on this side by a single unit, on the side of Sanski Most, and I asked the commander what the main axis was of the enemy attack and the answer I was given was that that is the main road between Sanski Most and Prijedor. Since my battalion was the first one to be coming in and I said I am going to go on that axis, and I was determined to defend it to the very last.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a nice way you tried to tell us here, these Muslim soldiers who were attacking Prijedor, how did they behave towards Serb civilians who remained in the areas that they were taking? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not have any knowledge. I just had assumptions. However, later on, the people of Sanski Most who fled at the very last moment, they saw those who could not move fast or could not run, they saw how they lost their lives. Believe me, it is hard to describe this in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, thank you. This is all that we had for you at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Zec, any matters? But I'm first looking at my colleagues. No questions from the Bench. Has the re-examination triggered any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Only one question if you allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one question. Please proceed. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Zec:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, Mr. Lukic asked you whether members of your battalion participated in interrogation of prisoners at Keraterm, and you were explaining they were not there. But this task of interrogating prisoners at Keraterm, that was in fact responsibility of the members of the 43rd Motorised Brigade for -- organ for security and intelligence. So that's -- that's was, in fact, the task assigned to this organ of the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to answer you in the way that the Trial Chamber has requested me to do. I will say that I disagree with that. The crime prevention police of Prijedor was carrying out the interrogations in Keraterm. Only those interrogations that were carried out by the military service took place during their arrest. And then on the basis of the statements, it was assessed whether they would be sent home or whether they would be sent to Keraterm or Omarska. So the army did not take part in any kind of interrogation in Keraterm itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Defence witness Miso Rodic testified here about how the interrogations would handle the situation and in contact with people held in Keraterm, including civilians, how they had visible signs of beatings and physical violence. I take it that you don't have any knowledge about this; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched the testimony of Mr. Miso Rodic, and he said to you that he had this interrogation in the offices of the military police where his office was too and on two or three occasions at the brigade command. Again, this does not pertain to Keraterm at all. You probably confused things there a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, finally, this office of the military police, that was just the location across the road from Keraterm; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question. There is something that is unclear to me there in what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The military police, they were located in the building across from Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that as well. It was the military command that was opposite. And the military police building was right by the Keraterm building but it could not have been entered from the Keraterm yard. Rather, only from the then-brick factory direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, from where did you watch the testimony of Mr. Miso Rodic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Internet. I found his testimony. And I know that he testified via videolink and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No further questions. Mr. Vujic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, that were put to you by the parties, were you put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the Defence is ready to call its next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the next witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, there was one document remaining MFI'd where you announced, Mr. Lukic, that you would deal with it in -- in re-examination. That was P7368. But I think you didn't do that. Which means that it's still now then pending a decision on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't have answer to that, Your Honour. But with help of my colleague, Kandice Ardiel, who is with us today, I'm able to respond to this P7126 that was actually -- said that Mr. Lukic, who testified on the 9th and 10th September, 2014, confirmed that there was a census. He was never shown this document and the document was introduced only on the 12th of February, 2015, through the witness Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it is in evidence, and let me just try to remember what happened with Mr. Puhalic. The document was tendered through Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You then did not object. And then after it was already admitted, you suddenly said, Sorry for being late but I want to object. Then Mr. Traldi said -- well, at least it was clear that it was provenance and authorship, and then Mr. Traldi would give you that during the break. And we gave you a possibility to revisit your objections, to substantiate them after the break once you had received that information and we never heard from you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only -- but the same witness, Mr. Puhalic, through this document was introduced said that he was not aware of any census [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All fine. Let me just first --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness put his earphones on. Whatever is the case, you had an opportunity then to raise it. You were invited to do so and you didn't say anything about it any further. Good afternoon, Mr. Trkulja, I take it? Mr. Trkulja, I'm speaking to you, that is the Presiding Judge, just in front of you. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Trkulja. Mr. Trkulja, you'll ... Mr. Trkulja, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for the Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, you know the rules. No greeting. And your invitation for Mr. Stojanovic to move a little bit further away so that you could have direct eye contact with the witness is not what you're supposed to do, once again, and you know that that will be the consequence. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to state your full name and surname slowly for the record.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Nedeljko Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1942, village of Grkovci, municipality of Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just tell the Trial Chamber in which republic of the former Yugoslavia Grahovo is.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber where you live today.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I live in Leskovac, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, could you briefly describe your professional education and your military career until you retired.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness. Could all other microphones please be switched off and could the witness please be asked to speak louder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- Witness. Witness, we had difficulty -- the interpreters had difficulties in hearing you. Could you therefore restart your answer, speaking at a bit higher volume, and you were asked -- you were invited to briefly describe your professional education and your military career until retirement. Could you restart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovic, you are requested to switch off your microphone while the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I graduated from the command staff academy and before that the school for non-commissioned officers. I started my military career as platoon leader in Skopje, then commander of a company, then deputy commander of a battalion. I was a battalion commander then. Then assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training, then Chief of Staff. Then chief of armoured units of the Kumanovo Corps, then the Leskovac Corps, and then finally chief of armoured units of the Army of Republika Srpska. After that, I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber when you joined the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: On the 10th of December, 19 -- no. 1993. 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did that happen? How come in December 1993? How come you were sent to the Army of Republika Srpska then?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That's when I received an order from the 30th Personnel Centre and that was linked to the position I had there. The brigade was disbanded and until it boiled down to zero, they wouldn't let me leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you were sent to the Army of Republika Srpska, did it have anything to do with your origins and the place where you were born?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That alone. That is what all the people who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina got.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please describe to us what the situation was like in December 1993 in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska as far as the establishment of the Main Staff was concerned and the extent to which it was manned?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The level of manning was about 40 per cent. For example, there were no desk officers for any one of the chiefs of services. The operations organ did not have a single desk officer so it was only the chiefs that there were. And when I say "40 per cent," that is that, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the capacity for accommodation at the Main Staff and where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The capacity for accommodation of the staff organs was such that we stayed there. It was at a very low level. There were three of us in one room, and that was what we had. All the facilities were at a very low level. These were quite old prefabricated buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who gave you your establishment deployment in 1993 when you came to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The personnel officer at the Main Staff. He was the one who did the scheduling. It was -- he was at the hotel in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We find it very difficult to understand and hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you try to raise your volume and come closer to the microphone because otherwise your words will be lost and ... yes? Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what the specific duties were of the chief of the service such as the service of the armoured and mechanized units of the VRS where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: We all had to have our work cards for the personnel and for the equipment and then there would be review. And then on the basis of that, requests would be made. If it was about equipment, that would be going through the technical organ for repairs, for example. The use of units was done in such a way that we did not have any armoured units that were immediately subordinated to the Main Staff. We would suggest their use. The proposal could be adopted or not. It was up to the superior command to make these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that we proposed how the units should be used, did the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in the period from December 1991 until the end of the war have anything like these types of mechanised units?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The staff did not have any immediately subordinated armoured units in their composition. There were armoured units but they were under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the other corps of the Army of Republika Srpska? Did they have armoured and mechanized units?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but they were quite small.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you, as the chief of service of the VRS armoured mechanized units, who were you subordinated to at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: We were subordinated to the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move to a different topic that is of interest to us. What did you spend most of your time on? What were your duties in the operational sense at the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Since the units were understaffed, we were busy in monitoring all the units, not just the mechanized units. We would constantly be monitoring the combat readiness and the capacities of all the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this process of reporting back to the Main Staff of the VRS on a daily basis, how did that go on? How did you report to them about the situation on the front throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The reports would arrive in the evening -- or they would -- the process of writing the reports would finish late in the evening. And then in the morning, at 7.00, they would be sent to the Main Staff when they would be informed about the situation at the front and about anything that they would need to be informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the reports would arrive from the corps of the Army of Republika Srpska from the field to the VRS Main Staff, what would then be the duty of the operations organ of the Main Staff of the VRS? What would they do then once they received these reports?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I said from the beginning that the operations organ was fully staffed so that the bulk of those reports were drafted by me. First of all, I would need to report -- receive reports from all the corps. Then I would make a summary for each corps. Then I would put them all together in one report which would then be sent back to all the corps and the president of the republic. And this was signed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And these reports that you drafted very frequently, were they summaries of those reports that you received from the corps of Republika Srpska for that day?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak up and repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this report would be drafted exclusively on the basis of these other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, sir, did it ever happen that due to fierce combat in certain sectors of the front, at any point in time, you would receive interim combat reports from any of the corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, that would happen, but not very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when such an interim report was arrived -- would arrive in those rare situations, what would be your duties at the Main Staff? Would you need to pass that on to the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander and to the other corps for their information?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot specifically say because I never encountered such situations. If any situation -- meaning any situation where a problem needed to be resolved immediately. This was something that went straight to Milovanovic and then I don't know what happened from that point on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this entire process of compiling information from the corps, summarising them and putting them all into one report which would then be sent to the corps and to the president of the republic, how much did General Mladic participate in this process at all as the Supreme Commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, not at all. The reports would be arriving in starting from 7.00 a.m. Somebody would be drafting them. They would be taken to the typist. They would be typed, taken to Milovanovic for his signature, and then they would be messengered over for encryption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you put a question to the witness which is, by the way, very leading, like many of the questions, but then you suggest already when you said, "Would you need to pass that on to the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander," if the witness then does not confirm that, then to continue in one of your next questions as if he would have confirmed that, that means that apparently you're more interested in the questions than in the answers the witness gives. That's not how it should be. So please refrain from leading extremely. Second, if the witness denies something or doesn't confirm something, either seek to clarify but do not just ignore his answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I will do my best because this answer denying or negating it referred to interim combat reports and the question was about regular combat reports. So perhaps that's where the confusion comes from and I will try to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether or not it was just about the interim reports -- I read it differently but you may clarify that. But, again, I think the witness has not at any point in time - but please correct me when I'm wrong - has stated that the normal reports were sent to the Supreme Commander. But I leave it in your hands. But please be aware that we are carefully following how you put questions because that may have an effect on the probative value of the evidence you are leading. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to clarify that by putting a question, but I think we'll find the relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, to whom were these regular reports sent once you put them all into one report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: They would go to the Supreme Commander and to all the corps in order to inform them about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question that I put to you was: How much did General Mladic participate as the chief of the Main Staff in this whole process? Did your answer refer to this process of regular reporting to the Supreme Commander about daily events at the front?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I explained completely the procedure, how it went from the drafting to the dispatch of it. General Mladic did not participate at all in this process. This was signed by Milovanovic and then it would be sent by messenger to the encryption area. The messenger would then take the typed report that was supposed to be sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And generally speaking, how much time did General Mladic physically spend at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: In essence, it was relatively little. Not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when General Mladic was not there, who was authorised to issue specific orders then?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Exclusively General Milovanovic. And no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to focus on July 1995. Did you personally, as the chief of the armoured mechanized units of the Army of Republika Srpska, in any way participate or were you acquainted with the course of the Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. I wasn't, and neither was any of my colleagues, the chief of services. Otherwise I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I simply rise because we're entering -- counsel is entering into July 1995, and this witness has in the past and I think it is appropriate for him to receive a Rule 90(E) caution. I intended to do that during my cross, but clearly this is going to be the bulk of his testimony from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I don't know what questions you have on your mind, but if you do not oppose, then I would follow the suggestion of Ms. Hasan. Witness, I'll read to you Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate that witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Which means, if you think that a truthful answer might incriminate yourself, then you may address me and ask to be relieved from your duty to answer that question. If you answer a question, it should always be truthful. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, do you personally know whether any chiefs of the services at the Main Staff participated in any actions regarding the planning of the Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I said just now that I don't have any information about it. I didn't even know the name. The first time I heard of that name was in 1997, and it was in this courtroom here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you physically in mid-July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I was at the command post, and it was an underground shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify one matter, you said you heard for the first time in 1997 when you testified in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not -- I'm sorry. Not 1997. It was 2007. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the reason why I asked you about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, I'd like to take you back for a second to one of the previous matters, that was about the reporting system where you said Mr. Mladic hardly had to do anything with it. Now, those reports which you say were sent to -- I think to General Milovanovic and then directly to the Supreme Commander, being the president of the Republika Srpska, does that mean that the -- that Mr. Mladic was not informed about such reports? Did he -- was he not copied on it? Was it just sent to Mr. Karadzic at the time without Mr. Mladic knowing about it? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the reports, that is how you should understand that. I don't know whether he received reports by phone. That's something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he was not the addressee of a copy of those reports. It just passed by him without him even being made acquainted with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, when he went to the operations room, he could ask to see a report if he wanted to. Sometimes it is returned from the encoders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so the fact that he was not directly addressed, you say doesn't mean that he was not aware of the content. He may well have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he could have found out. He could have gone downstairs the next day and taken a look at it. But the report was not sent directly to him, and he did not participate in the drafting or sending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Now I'd like to move on to a document. I have several questions in relation to this document so that will take a while, so please tell me whether I should start that now or whether we should adjourn at this point and continue tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it would take us beyond quarter past 2.00, then I think it's better to adjourn a bit earlier. Mr. Trkulja, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.30. But before you leave this courtroom, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, the Chamber noted that it seems to have become a tendency to increase the time for witnesses where it is rather unclear what exactly causes that, why a witness who is scheduled for one hour now suddenly needs one hour and a half, or one hour and a half suddenly needs two hours. The Chamber is concerned about it, and invites the Defence to either better explain or refrain from adding time where a time has been assessed for the witness previously. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume -- Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this digression pertains to my questioning of the witness Nedeljko Trkulja, I did ask for an extension of about 15 minutes. I believe that I won't even be needing that. However, I had to exercise caution because during the proofing, in view of everything he said, I felt it was necessary to use another document, a Prosecution document, and I thought that it would be necessary for me to inform you that I might be using this additional 15 minutes. I apologise for that. I would like to use this opportunity, now that we have time until the end of our working hours today, today is our deadline to respond to the Prosecution motion to include part of the transcript of Grujo Bojic according to Rule 80(C) [as interpreted]. We dealt with the matter and the position of the Defence is to say, for the record, that the Defence is going to oppose this, namely that parts of the transcripts of Mr. Boric be admitted in this way on the basis of Rule 89(C), that is to say, what he stated as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to say that it is entire clear to me, not yet, but I'll re-read the transcript and see. Mr. Stojanovic, if it is -- if this was just an incident, you have explained it, the 15 days. I was more talking about the routine rather than -- 15 minutes. What did I say? 15 days, no, certainly not. 15 minutes. I was -- I was expressing the concern of the Chamber by it becoming more and more routine to extend the time. That was what I wanted to draw your attention to. We adjourn for the day. We resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 5th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
